title: Ten Handbreadths as a Domain, Then the Ark's Missing Measurement
subtitle: Why 10 tefachim is a real boundary in the first place, then a long hunt for how tall the Ark's cover actually was.
sources: Gemara text: Sefaria (William Davidson Edition). Structure and quiz questions 1-3 cross-checked against the Dafyomi Advancement Forum (dafyomi.co.il) quiz for Sukkah 5. Tosfos: dafyomi.co.il's "Point by Point Summary of Tosfos" (Yaakov Montrose, Kollel Iyun Hadaf). The Tzitz discussion continues onto 5b.
before: 4b ended by asking where the Mishnah's 10-tefachim minimum height comes from. This amud opens with a striking proof: a beraita claiming the Divine Presence never actually descended below 10 tefachim, and Moshe and Eliyahu never actually ascended above it — establishing 10 tefachim up as a genuinely separate domain.

From there the Gemara chases down one specific number: the Ark of the Covenant was 9 tefachim tall by an explicit verse, but its cover (kaporet) needed one more tefach to reach 10 — and nowhere does the Torah say how thick the cover was. The rest of the amud is that hunt: several failed derivations, then two that work.

flow.label: Beraita: the Divine Presence never came below 10 tefachim; Moshe and Eliyahu never rose above it
flow.sub: every apparent counter-verse gets reread as "stayed within 10 tefachim of the boundary"

flow.label: Payoff: 10 tefachim really is a separate domain
flow.sub: so a sukkah under 10 tefachim isn't a domain of its own — that's why it's invalid

flow.label: Where the 10-tefachim number comes from: Ark (9) + Cover (1) = 10
flow.sub: the Ark's own height is explicit in the verse — the cover's thickness is not

flow.label: Failed derivations for the cover's thickness

items.label: From the smallest Mishkan vessel with a stated measure (the table's border)
items.sub: actually works — the one the Gemara keeps

items.label: From the High Priest's frontplate / a crown
items.sub: rejected — those are ornaments, not vessels, so they can't set a vessel's measure

flow.label: Gemara notices the winning derivation itself has a loose thread
flow.sub: was the table's border above the tabletop or below? Only "below" cleanly supports the proof — continues onto 5b

flowCaption: One clean proof that 10 tefachim is a real domain, then a careful hunt for a single missing measurement.

opinions.claim: The Divine Presence never actually descended below 10 tefachim, and Moshe and Eliyahu never actually ascended above it — every verse that looks otherwise stayed within 10 tefachim of the boundary.
opinions.basis: "The heavens are the heavens of the Lord, and the earth He gave to the children of man" (Psalms 115:16) — two distinct domains, split at 10 tefachim.

opinions.claim: An alternative derivation, independent of the table's border: "upon the face (penei) of the Ark cover" — and no person's face measures less than a tefach.
opinions.basis: A verbal analogy (gezerah shavah-style) between "penei" here and "penei" elsewhere, refined via the cherubs' faces rather than a literal human face.

script.speaker: Beraita
script.quote: מֵעוֹלָם לֹא יָרְדָה שְׁכִינָה לְמַטָּה, וְלֹא עָלוּ מֹשֶׁה וְאֵלִיָּהוּ לַמָּרוֹם.
script.gloss: Rabbi Yosei: the Divine Presence never actually descended below (10 tefachim), and Moshe and Eliyahu never actually ascended above it — the heavens and earth are two distinct domains.

script.speaker: Gemara challenges, repeatedly
script.gloss: Doesn't a verse say God descended onto Mount Sinai? Won't His feet stand on the Mount of Olives? Didn't Moshe go up to God, and Eliyahu ascend in a whirlwind? Each time, the Gemara answers the same way: whatever the verse describes, it stopped at the 10-tefachim line — descending to it, or rising to it, but never crossing.

script.speaker: One more push
script.gloss: But a verse says Moshe "grasped the face of the Throne" — doesn't that mean he touched something above the 10-tefachim line?

script.speaker: Answered
script.quote: אִישְׁתַּרְבּוֹבֵי אִישְׁתַּרְבַּב לֵיהּ כִּסֵּא עַד עֲשָׂרָה, וּנְקַט בֵּיהּ.
script.gloss: The Throne itself stretched down to the 10-tefachim line so Moshe could grasp it — he himself never crossed it.

script.speaker: The number, sourced
script.quote: בִּשְׁלָמָא אָרוֹן תִּשְׁעָה... אֶלָּא כַּפּוֹרֶת טֶפַח, מְנָלַן?
script.gloss: The Ark itself was 9 tefachim tall — stated explicitly (a cubit and a half, Exodus 25:10). But where does the extra tefach for the cover's thickness come from? The Torah never states it.

script.speaker: First derivation
script.quote: צֵא וּלְמַד מִפָּחוּת שֶׁבַּכֵּלִים... מָה לְהַלָּן טֶפַח, אַף כָּאן טֶפַח.
script.gloss: Learn from the smallest Mishkan vessel-dimension the Torah states: the show-bread table's border (misgeret) is explicitly one tefach — so the cover's thickness is a tefach too. The Gemara adds the principle behind picking the smallest available source: "if you grasp for more, you grasp nothing; grasp for less, and you have something."

script.speaker: Two rejected alternatives
script.gloss: Why not derive the thickness from the High Priest's golden frontplate (just two fingerbreadths), or from a vessel's decorative crown (no fixed size at all)? Both are rejected: a vessel's measure can only be derived from another vessel's measure — not from an ornament, and not from mere decorative finish.

script.speaker: A wrinkle in the winning proof
script.gloss: The border-derivation only cleanly works for the view that the table's border sat below the tabletop, supporting it structurally as a real functional part of the vessel. For the view that it sat above, it looks like mere decoration too — continued on 5b.

tosfos.summary: Why spelling out "Yud-Heh" isn't a violation, even though it's part of God's name.

points.label: (b) Answer #1
points.he: כיון דאינו מזכירם לשם שם שלם
points.en: Because he isn't saying these letters with intent that they form a complete name.

points.label: (c) Answer #2
points.he: ההוגה שם באותיותיו פירש בקונטרס שדורש אותיות של שם בן ארבעים ושתים
points.en: Rashi explains the actual prohibition applies specifically to spelling out the 42-letter name, not this.

tosfos.summary: A dense side-discussion (condensed here) about whether the table's border sat above or below it, and what that implies for which wooden objects can become ritually impure.

points.label: (a)-(b) Two readings
points.he: ולא כמו שמפרש ר״ת דלמאן דאמר למטה היתה מחוברת נמי בשלחן
points.en: The Gemara's own wording implies that on the "below" view, the border wasn't just decorative — it was a structural rim the tabletop rested on. Rabbeinu Tam reads it differently, tying the question to a separate sugya (Menachos 96b) about when a flippable board can become impure.

points.label: (j) Answer
points.he: כל הני לא דמו לדף של נחתום מחמת שהדפין רחבין וראוי להניח עליהן דבר גזרו עליהן
points.en: The resolution: ordinary flat wooden boards stay pure even rabbinically, but a baker's board is wide enough to functionally hold things, so the Sages treated it like a container — which is why it can become impure specifically on the "border below" reading.

tosfos.summary: Whether the High Priest's frontplate (tzitz) sat on the forehead or higher up on the head — condensed.

points.label: (b) Answer
points.he: אין זה אלא מדרבנן משום דכתיב על מצחו שיעור מצחו
points.en: The earlier "two fingerbreadths" measure is only rabbinic, tied to the verse "on his forehead" — an average forehead's width.

points.label: (c)-(d) The Riva's view
points.he: ריב״א מפרש הציץ היה מונח בראש... דשל כהן הדיוט גדולה משל כהן גדול שהציץ היה דוחה אותה
points.en: The Riva holds the tzitz actually sat higher, on the head rather than the forehead — pointing to why the High Priest's headwear is called by a different term than the ordinary priest's, since the tzitz pushed against it. Continued on 5b.
